note: Reader-facing annotations for the fragmentation comparison (D8), extracted from each guide's population.note (carried on City.population.note per D23). EXTRACTION RULE: keep the factual municipal-history or population-trend clause; drop census-vintage provenance and every reference to the guide's own authoring decisions ('fragmentationRatio left null...', 'consistent with the caveat practice established in the ... JSON files', 'flagged as a possible Field Notes follow-up'). No fact is added, sharpened, or reworded beyond compression. `sourceNote` is the original verbatim so the trimming stays auditable — see design/m5a-data-page.md.

kinds.mechanism: A structural reason the city-proper/metro ratio is what it is.
kinds.trend: A population trajectory that qualifies how the ratio should be read.
kinds.none: The guide's note is census-vintage provenance only — no annotation is rendered rather than padding one.

atlanta-ga.mechanism: A nationally cited case study in municipal fragmentation: Sandy Springs, Brookhaven, Dunwoody, Milton and others incorporated out of unincorporated Fulton and DeKalb counties from 2005, largely to control local tax base and schools.
atlanta-ga.sourceNote: City-proper figure is a recent-estimate midpoint (2020 census: 498,715); metro figure is the Atlanta-Sandy Springs-Alpharetta MSA, both pending Census reconciliation. fragmentationRatio left null: Atlanta metro is a nationally cited case study in municipal fragmentation via the 'cityhood movement' (Sandy Springs, Brookhaven, Dunwoody, Milton and others incorporating out of unincorporated Fulton/DeKalb County since 2005, largely to control local tax base and schools) but no single ratio has been computed for this guide -- flagged as a possible Field Notes follow-up rather than a number invented for this file.

oklahoma-city-ok.mechanism: The metric inverts here: OKC annexed aggressively rather than fragmenting, producing a city-proper land area of roughly 620 square miles — one of the largest municipal footprints in the country — and the same outcome by the opposite route.
oklahoma-city-ok.sourceNote: OKC city-proper land area is roughly 620 sq mi — one of the largest municipal footprints in the country. The fragmentation metric inverts here relative to the Southern corridor: OKC annexed aggressively rather than fragmenting, which produced a different mechanism for the same outcome. Figures are approximate estimates pending Census reconciliation.

washington-dc.mechanism: Structurally unlike the rest: the District cannot annex or be annexed and has no county government at all, and Congress retains ultimate budget authority regardless of city-proper boundaries.
washington-dc.sourceNote: City-proper figure is a 2023-vintage estimate; metro figure rounds the Washington-Arlington-Alexandria MSA. DC's fragmentation metric is structurally different from the Southern corridor's -- the city cannot annex or be annexed, and has no county government at all, since Congress retains ultimate budget authority over the District regardless of city-proper boundaries. Figures are approximate, pending Census reconciliation, consistent with prior JSON files' caveat practice.

dallas-tx.mechanism: A genuinely polycentric metro — Fort Worth, Arlington and Plano are independent city governments rather than annexed Dallas territory, a different fragmentation mechanism from Oklahoma City's aggressive annexation.
dallas-tx.sourceNote: City-proper and DFW-metro figures are approximate mid-2020s estimates pending Census reconciliation; DFW is a genuinely polycentric metro (Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, etc. are independent city governments, not annexed Dallas territory), which is a different fragmentation mechanism than OKC's aggressive-annexation pattern noted in that city's file. No fragmentation ratio has been computed here — left null rather than guessed.

las-vegas-nv.mechanism: Unincorporated Clark County holds much of the built-up Las Vegas Valley — including the Strip itself — outside city-proper limits, which understates the city's functional footprint against its metro.
las-vegas-nv.sourceNote: City-proper and metro figures are approximate estimates pending Census reconciliation. Clark County unincorporated areas (much of the actual built-up Las Vegas Valley, including the Strip itself) fall outside city-proper limits, which understates the city's functional footprint relative to its metro population.

richmond-va.mechanism: Virginia's independent-city structure makes Richmond's own boundary unusually stable compared with the annexation and fragmentation patterns elsewhere on the corridor.
richmond-va.sourceNote: City-proper and metro figures are estimates (Richmond city + Chesterfield/Henrico/Hanover-anchored metro) pending Census reconciliation; Virginia's independent-city structure makes Richmond's own boundary unusually stable compared to Southern-corridor annexation/fragmentation cities, so fragmentationRatio is left null rather than forced.

jackson-ms.mechanism: Jackson's population has declined meaningfully since 2020 amid the city's prolonged water-system crisis and out-migration; the figure is a starting point, not a current count.
jackson-ms.sourceNote: 2020 Census baseline. Jackson's population has declined meaningfully since 2020 amid the city's prolonged water-system crisis and out-migration; treat these figures as a starting point pending Census reconciliation, not a current count.

charlotte-nc.mechanism: One of the fastest-growing large US cities, so the true current city-proper figure is almost certainly higher than the estimate shown.
charlotte-nc.sourceNote: City-proper figure is the 2023 Census estimate; Charlotte has been one of the fastest-growing large US cities so the true 2026 figure is almost certainly higher. Metro figure is the Charlotte-Concord-Gastonia, NC-SC MSA 2023 estimate. Both pending Census reconciliation.

birmingham-al.mechanism: The city-proper figure sits on a declining post-2020 base.
birmingham-al.sourceNote: City-proper figure is a 2023-era estimate off a declining post-2020-Census base; metro figure (Birmingham-Hoover MSA) is rounded. Both should be reconciled against a single Census vintage before publication.

shreveport-la.mechanism: Shreveport-proper has declined from a 2010 peak of roughly 199,000.
shreveport-la.sourceNote: Figures are approximate estimates pending Census reconciliation, consistent with the caveat practice established in the Oklahoma City and Dallas JSON files. Shreveport-proper has declined from a 2010 peak (~199,000); the metro figure is the Shreveport-Bossier City MSA.

albuquerque-nm.sourceNote: City-proper figure is the 2020 Census count; metro figure is a rounded 2023-era estimate for the Albuquerque MSA. Both are approximate pending reconciliation against a single census vintage.

boise-id.sourceNote: Figures are approximate estimates pending Census reconciliation, consistent with the caveat practice established in the Oklahoma City and Dallas JSON files.
